newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist PM retreats under army pressure.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist PM retreats under army pressure.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan resigned on Wednesday, bringing to a close a tempestuous one-year tenure as the modern republic's first Islamist leader.
"A short while ago I presented my resignation to the president," Erbakan, apparently unbowed, told reporters after a 45-minute meeting with President Suleyman Demirel.
"Our country will now be freed of a false agenda and useless, needless tensions," he said.

His resignation, eagerly awaited by both his secularist critics and his putative coalition partners, was part of a delicate power-sharing deal designed to ease the pressure on the government and lead the country to early elections.

But a series of political and procedural obstacles, aggravated by the army's public displeasure with his Islamist leanings, could yet block Erbakan's bid to hand the prime minister's job to his secularist partner, Tansu Ciller.
"Turkey is heading towards an unknown period, a period where democracy is under threat," political commentator Bilal Cetin told Reuters.
Under Turkish law, the president is not bound by the wishes of the outgoing government, outlined in a letter signed by Erbakan, Ciller and the head of a far-right splinter party.
Consultations with individual party leaders were set to begin at the presidential palace on Thursday.

Erbakan's decision to stand down -- fueled by his confident prediction of future election triumphs -- came just hours before the expiration of a midnight deadline (2100 GMT) imposed by Ciller's conservative True Path Party.
And it capped a remarkable political struggle that mirrored a broader fight for secular but overwhelmingly Moslem Turkey's place in the modern world.

Erbakan, 70, and his Islam-based Welfare Party saw Turkey as a potential leader of an invigorated Moslem East, on a par with such Western institutions as NATO, the European Union and the International Monetary Fund.
In the event, his record since taking office in June of 1996 reflects little of the millenarian vision of his "Just Order" campaign manifesto.

Nor does it appear to justify the near-hysteria of the mainstream secularist press, which was quick to paint every initiative from Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party as the first step toward sectarian violence, Algerian-style.
Nonethless, Erbakan and Ciller were forced to watch their parliamentary majority melt away before the anti-Islamist onslaught led by the army brass.
This has left them at the mercy of a tiny rightist party with just eight MPs in order to win any vote of confidence for their "election" government, to be led by Ciller.

The military, which has toppled three governments in the last four decades, has publically pledged its readiness to turn back any threat to Turkey's secular order "by force of arms" -- tough talk that alarmed close ally the United States.

The press and business elite also fed the current anti-Islamist effort, sparking enough defections among MPs and ministers from among Ciller's conservatives to cost the coalition a majority in the 550-seat parliament.

Even Welfare, traditionally a bastion of party discipline, has seen its number of deputies fall, depriving it of valuable votes in the revamped coalition's bid for a confidence vote. Two radical Welfare MPs quit the party on Wednesday.
Erbakan's tenure, now apparently at an end, saw a harried leader effectively blocked by army pressure from introducing Islamist reforms and building bridges to Turkey's Moslem neighbours.
He presided at the weekend over the founding summit in Istanbul of the Developing-Eight (D-8) Moslem nations, a watered down version of his campaign pledge to head a new Islamic power bloc.

But he has been helpless to limit Turkey's long-standing role in NATO and to stop growing military ties with Israel that have angered the Arabs. Five Turkish navy vessels docked in an Israeli port on Monday in defiance of the prime minister's pro-Arab stance.
